clusters.name: Structural functionalism
clusters.fact: Structural functionalism sees society as a system of interdependent parts that work together to maintain stability and cohesion.

manifest function.text: Merton's term for a social practice's intended, recognized purpose — contrasted with its latent, unintended effects.
manifest function.link: wiki:Manifest and latent functions and dysfunctions

latent function.link: wiki:Manifest and latent functions and dysfunctions

info.text: A perspective in sociology that treats society as a system of interdependent parts, each contributing to the stability of the whole — much like organs in a body.

clusters.name: Conflict theory
clusters.fact: Conflict theory sees society as an arena of competition, where groups struggle over scarce resources and power.

power.text: The ability to influence or control the behavior of others — who holds it is conflict theory's central question.

inequality.text: Unequal access to resources, opportunities, and rewards across groups in a society.

false consciousness.text: A Marxist concept: a mindset where people fail to recognize the inequality and exploitation built into their own social class position.

info.text: A perspective in sociology that views society as an ongoing contest between groups with different levels of resources, status, and influence.

clusters.name: Symbolic interactionism
clusters.fact: Symbolic interactionism studies how individuals create meaning through everyday symbols and face-to-face interaction.

dramaturgy.text: Goffman's idea that everyday social life resembles a theatrical performance, with people managing the impression they give others.

micro-level interaction.text: Face-to-face, everyday interaction between individuals — the small scale symbolic interactionism studies, as opposed to whole institutions or societies.

info.text: A perspective in sociology that focuses on how individuals build shared understanding through everyday interaction and the cues they exchange.

bridges.fact: Socialization bridges the two: functionalists see it as teaching shared norms that hold society together, while conflict theorists see the same process as reproducing existing inequality across generations.

Deviance bridges the two: conflict theorists see who gets labeled deviant as a reflection of who holds power, while interactionists focus on how that labeling itself, through everyday interaction, shapes a person's identity.

info.text: Behavior that violates a society's norms — sociologists study who gets labeled deviant, and why, rather than treating the label as neutral.
